idiom_name: Thread::SizedQueue(max): push blocks when full, pop blocks when empty
implementation_notes: Ruby's standard library ships the whole mechanism: Thread::SizedQueue.new(max) is a bounded queue whose push/<< blocks the producer when the queue is at capacity and whose pop blocks the consumer when it is empty, so the classic monitor/lock structure is never written. Thread::Queue is the same class without the bound (an unbounded queue, and therefore the failure mode the pattern prevents); use SizedQueue by default and reach for Thread::Queue only when the backlog is genuinely unbounded. Fibers and Enumerator::Lazy are the pull alternative - a lazy chain consumes on demand so no explicit signal is needed - and Ractor ports would be the cross-actor form, but SizedQueue remains the canonical realization.
code_sketch:
frames = Thread::SizedQueue.new(64)      # bounded hand-off

producer = Thread.new { src.each { |f| frames.push(f) } }   # blocks when full
consumer = Thread.new do
  while (frame = frames.pop)           # blocks when empty
    process(frame)
  end
end
[producer, consumer].each(&:join)
pitfalls: Thread::Queue (unbounded) is what most examples use; switching to SizedQueue is the entire bound.
An exception in the producer thread leaves the consumer blocked on pop forever - report_on_exception and explicit shutdown sentinels are required.
SizedQueue#pop on an empty queue blocks the thread; the non-blocking form (pop(true)) raises ThreadError, so a polling consumer must handle that instead of assuming nil.
Ruby threads are OS threads under the GVL, so backpressure bounds memory and latency but does not make CPU-bound stages parallel.
